nameStory: The name 'hawkbit' comes from an old belief that hawks would eat these plants to sharpen their eyesight - though this is just folklore! The 'hairy' part of the name refers to the fuzzy texture you'll feel when you run your fingers along the leaves and stems.
description: Hairy Hawkbit is a small, dandelion-like wildflower that forms low rosettes of leaves close to the ground. From these leaf clusters, it sends up slender, leafless stems topped with bright yellow flowers that look remarkably similar to dandelions. The whole plant is quite petite, with leaves typically 2-6 inches long and flower stems reaching about the same height.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads made entirely of ray petals (no center disc), with each petal having tiny teeth at the tip - run your finger along a petal edge to feel these small notches

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves form a flat rosette at ground level and feel noticeably hairy or fuzzy to the touch, may be smooth-edged or have shallow lobes

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Flower stems are completely leafless and rise directly from the ground-level rosette, unlike branching stems of many similar plants

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Seeds have feathery white plumes like dandelions but form a smaller, less fluffy seed head that feels more papery than silky

habitat: Look for Hairy Hawkbit in disturbed soils, roadsides, and waste areas where it has been accidentally introduced from Europe. It prefers sunny spots with poor to average soil and good drainage. In New England, it's quite rare with only a few documented sightings.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in a tight rosette, feeling distinctly fuzzy and appearing bright green against bare soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with yellow flowers opening on sunny days - the leafless stems make identification easier now.
seasonality.fall: Seeds develop their feathery plumes and disperse on autumn winds, while leaves may persist in milder weather.
seasonality.winter: In protected areas, some basal leaves may survive under snow, appearing as small fuzzy rosettes when exposed.

funFact: Unlike dandelions that can close and reopen their flowers multiple times, Hairy Hawkbit flowers typically open just once - so if you see one closed on a sunny day, it's probably done blooming forever!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with dandelions, but Hairy Hawkbit feels much fuzzier when you touch the leaves and has smaller, more delicate flowers. The flower stems are also proportionally thinner and the seed heads are less robust-looking than dandelion puff balls.
contextualKnowledge: Though called a 'weed' in its introduced range, Hairy Hawkbit is actually quite rare in New England with only three recorded observations. Don't assume every small yellow flower that looks like a dandelion actually is one - many different plants have evolved this successful flower design!
compareHints: Hairy Hawkbit is the only hawkbit species documented in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other dandelion-like plants in the Asteraceae family, it's distinguished by its consistently hairy texture and smaller, more delicate overall appearance with proportionally thinner flower stems.
